readings.title: King Alfred and the Beggar
readings.challenge: Connect a kind act early in the day with what happens that night and the next morning.
readings.focus: Sharing half of the last loaf is followed by good luck, a vision and a victory.
readings.context: King Alfred ruled part of England more than a thousand years ago, when the Danes, raiders from across the sea, were attacking it; a school night told another story about him, King Alfred and the cakes. Baldwin printed hyphens inside longer words to help young readers sound them out. Bidden means told; to reign is to rule as king.

excerpt.locator: “King Alfred and the Beggar,” the whole story; opens “At one time the Danes drove King Alfred from his kingdom, and he had to lie hidden for a…”; closes “…And King Alfred ruled wisely and well over all his people for the rest of his days.”.

questions.prompt: How much food does the king have when the beggar comes, and how much does he give away?
facilitatorNotes: Only one loaf and a little wine, and he gives away half of each. Giving half of very little is a bigger gift than it sounds.
evidence: we have only one loaf and a little wine
Give half of the loaf and half of the wine to this poor man.

questions.prompt: What happens in the afternoon that makes everyone more hopeful?
facilitatorNotes: The fishermen come back with three boats full of fish, more than on any other day. The story puts this luck right after the gift; children can say whether they think the two are connected.
evidence: They had three boats full of fish

questions.prompt: Who does the old man in the light say he is?
facilitatorNotes: The one to whom Alfred gave half his food that day: the beggar. The storyteller admits it may have been a dream, though it seemed real to the king. Ask whether the story would mean something different if it were only a dream.
evidence: for I am the one to whom you gave this day the half of all the food that you had
It may all have been a dream

questions.prompt: Why do the soldiers cheer when Alfred tells them what he saw and heard?
facilitatorNotes: The promise of victory gives them hope, so they will follow him as long as they have strength. Some children may say the dream mattered less than the king’s trust in it.
evidence: they all cheered loudly, and said that they would follow him

readings.title: The Sons of William the Conqueror
readings.challenge: Compare three answers to the same question, then test a prediction against what happens.
readings.focus: Each prince’s choice of bird is read as a sign of the man he will become.
readings.context: William the Conqueror became King of England in 1066. Baldwin tells an old story about his three sons. A willful lad wants his own way; gallant means brave and dashing; prudent means careful and sensible; foretold means said ahead of time.
readings.contentNote: The ending tells briefly that one prince died in prison and another was killed while hunting.

excerpt.locator: “The Sons of William the Conqueror,” the whole story; opens “There was once a great king of England who was called Wil-liam the Con-quer-or, and he…”; closes “…by the King of England and the ruler of all the lands that his father had had in France.”.

questions.prompt: The wise men ask each prince exactly the same question. Why ask it the same way three times?
facilitatorNotes: So the answers can be compared fairly: only the boys’ choices differ. Hearing the question repeated makes each answer stand out.
evidence: the same ques-tions should be put to each

questions.prompt: Which bird does each son choose, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Robert, a hawk, because it reminds him of a bold knight; William, an eagle, because it is strong and feared by all other birds; Henry, a starling, because it is kind and never robs its neighbor.
evidence: I would rather be a hawk
It is feared by all other birds
it never tries to rob or abuse its neigh-bor

questions.prompt: Why might Henry’s answer surprise his brothers?
facilitatorNotes: He chooses a small, ordinary bird and gives kindness as his reason, not strength or fear. His quiet steps and his nickname, the Handsome Scholar, fit the choice.
evidence: with quiet steps and a sober, thought-ful look

questions.prompt: The story says things happened “very much as the wise men had foretold.” Did the birds really show the future, or did the king help make it come true?
facilitatorNotes: The king remembered the prediction when he divided his lands, giving Henry only gold, yet Henry still became king. Some children will trust the wise men; others will notice how the father’s choices shaped events. The text supports both.
evidence: Then he re-mem-bered what the wise men had told him
So it hap-pened in the end very much as the wise men had fore-told.

readings.title: The White Ship
readings.challenge: Notice how a storyteller turns a merry mood into sorrow, then hear a poet tell the same grief.
readings.focus: A night of music ends in a shipwreck; a prince turns back for his sister, and his father never smiles again.
readings.context: This follows the story of William the Conqueror’s sons: Henry, the Handsome Scholar, is now King of England. The White Ship sank in 1120. Baldwin ends with a poem by Felicia Hemans, an English poet of the early 1800s. A bark is a ship; festal means belonging to a feast; a tourney is a contest of knights.
readings.contentNote: A ship sinks at night and almost everyone aboard drowns, including the prince and his sister; the poem is about a father’s grief.

excerpt.locator: “The White Ship,” the whole story with the poem “He Never Smiled Again” that Baldwin prints after it; opens “King Henry, the Handsome Scholar, had one son, named William, whom he dearly loved. The…”; closes “Mrs. Hemans.”.

questions.prompt: Which details at the start make the voyage sound safe and happy?
facilitatorNotes: A smooth sea, fair winds, music and dancing, and a full moon to light the way. The cheerful details make the sudden crash more shocking.
evidence: The sea was smooth, the winds were fair, and no one thought of danger.

questions.prompt: Prince William is already safe in the small boat. Why does he order it back?
facilitatorNotes: He hears his little sister cry out and says she must be saved. He chooses her over his own safety; the story does not call it a mistake.
evidence: It is my little sister. She must be saved!

questions.prompt: The storyteller asks, “Would they be saved?” Why ask a question instead of simply telling us?
facilitatorNotes: It makes listeners wait and hope along with the people in the boat. Children may notice the earlier question too: where are those who were so glad a moment ago?
evidence: Would they be saved?
Ah, where now were those who had lately been so heart-free and glad?

questions.prompt: The poem ends every verse with the same line. What is it, and how does hearing it again and again make you feel?
facilitatorNotes: “He never smiled again.” Coming after feasts, music and knightly contests, it shows that nothing the king sees can change his grief. Some children hear it as sad, others as heavy and slow like a bell.
evidence: He never smiled again.

readings.title: King John and the Abbot, part 1: three questions
readings.challenge: Hear why a powerful person is angry, and decide whether the punishment fits.
readings.focus: A jealous king sets three impossible questions, and even the wisest scholars cannot help.
readings.context: King John ruled England from 1199 to 1216. Baldwin retells an old English ballad, a story told in song. An abbot is the head of an abbey, a community of monks; Oxford and Cambridge are famous old universities.
readings.contentNote: The king threatens to have the abbot’s head cut off.

excerpt.locator: “King John and the Abbot,” part I, “The Three Questions”; opens “There was once a king of England whose name was John. He was a bad king; for he was harsh…”; closes “…home to bid his friends and his brave knights good-by. For now he had not a week to live.”.

questions.prompt: What has the abbot done that makes King John angry?
facilitatorNotes: He lives grandly, with a hundred noblemen at dinner and fifty knights to serve. The king thinks no one should live better than the king; the abbot answers that he spends only what is his own.
evidence: no man in the land ought to live better than the king
I am spending nothing but what is my own

questions.prompt: What are the king’s three questions?
facilitatorNotes: How long the king will live, to within a day; how soon he can ride round the whole world; and what he is thinking. Each sounds impossible to answer.
evidence: just how long I shall live
how soon I shall ride round the whole world
you shall tell me what I think

questions.prompt: The king will not let the abbot finish his sentence. What does that show about him?
facilitatorNotes: “Not another word!” He has already made up his mind and does not want to hear the abbot’s side. It fits what the storyteller says about him at the very start.
evidence: Not another word!
He was the worst king that England ever had.

questions.prompt: Why can’t the professors at Oxford and Cambridge help the abbot?
facilitatorNotes: There is nothing about King John in their books. The questions are about one man’s life and thoughts, which no book can answer. Children may guess what kind of helper could do better.
evidence: there was nothing about King John in any of their books

readings.title: King John and the Abbot, part 2: three answers
readings.challenge: Explain how a clever answer can be true without being the answer the asker wanted.
readings.focus: A shepherd in disguise answers all three questions with wit and wins a pardon.
readings.context: Recap: King John, jealous of a rich abbot, threatened to cut off his head unless he could answer three questions in two weeks: how long the king will live, how soon he can ride round the world, and what the king is thinking. No scholar could help. Wit means quick, clever thinking; a pardon is forgiveness from punishment.

excerpt.locator: “King John and the Abbot,” part II, “The Three Answers”; opens “As the abbot was riding up the lane which led to his grand house, he met his shep-herd…”; closes “…home, you may tell the old abbot that you have brought him a free pardon from King John."”.

questions.prompt: The shepherd says “a fool may teach a wise man wit.” How does the rest of the story prove him right?
facilitatorNotes: A shepherd who cannot read or write answers what the professors could not. In this story, cleverness about people matters more than book learning.
evidence: a fool may teach a wise man wit
I can neither read nor write

questions.prompt: Why can the shepherd take the abbot’s place so easily?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone says he looks just like the abbot, and he borrows the gown, cap, staff, horse and servants.
evidence: everybody says that I look just like you

questions.prompt: Choose one of the shepherd’s three answers. Why is it true, even though it is a trick?
facilitatorNotes: The king will live until the day he dies; riding with the sun all day and night takes twenty-four hours; and the king does think he is talking to the abbot. Each answer is true but turns the question around.
evidence: until the day that you die, and not one day longer
You think that I am the Abbot of Can-ter-bur-y.

questions.prompt: The king who threatened the abbot now laughs and gives a pardon. Has he changed?
facilitatorNotes: He enjoys the joke and rewards the shepherd. Some children will say a good laugh changed his mind; others that he still treated the abbot unfairly at the start. Both can be argued from the story.
evidence: The king laughed loud and long.
a free pardon from King John

readings.title: A Story of Robin Hood
readings.challenge: Weigh a storyteller’s mixed judgment of a hero, then follow a rescue planned in disguise.
readings.focus: An outlaw who robs the rich helps a heartbroken young man win his bride.
readings.context: Robin Hood is a hero of old English songs and legends; Sherwood Forest is in the middle of England. An outlaw is someone who has broken the law and lives outside it; a harper plays the harp; a match here means a marriage. The verse at the end comes from one of the old songs.

excerpt.locator: “A Story of Robin Hood,” the whole story; opens “In the rude days of King Rich-ard and King John there were many great woods in England.…”; closes “…a queen: And so they re-turned to the merry green wood, Amongst the leaves so green."”.

questions.prompt: What rules does Robin Hood follow with his band?
facilitatorNotes: He divides everything fairly, harms only rich men who do no work, and is kind to the poor. These rules are why common people thought of him as a friend.
evidence: He then di-vid-ed it fairly among them
He was always kind to the poor

questions.prompt: Baldwin says some people praised Robin Hood and some blamed him. What does Baldwin himself think?
facilitatorNotes: He calls him “a rude, lawless fellow,” but says people then thought about right and wrong differently. Children can say whether a robber can also be a hero.
evidence: Some praised him, and some blamed him.
He was, indeed, a rude, lawless fellow

questions.prompt: How can Robin tell that something has gone wrong for the young man on the second day?
facilitatorNotes: He has left his scarlet coat at home and sighs and groans at every step instead of tripping along happily. His clothes and his walk tell the story before he does.
evidence: He had left his scarlet coat at home, and at every step he sighed and groaned.

questions.prompt: Robin says, “Let the bride choose for herself.” Why does that matter so much in this story?
facilitatorNotes: Her father had promised her to a rich old man she had never seen. Robin gives her the choice. Compare her pale cheeks and tears before with her blush when she chooses.
evidence: Let the bride choose for herself.
Her cheeks were very pale, and her eyes were full of tears.

readings.title: The Black Douglas
readings.challenge: Notice what readers know that the people in the story do not.
readings.focus: A mother’s lullaby about a feared enemy is answered by the enemy himself.
readings.context: Sir James Douglas fought for King Robert Bruce of Scotland against the English about seven hundred years ago (a school night told of Bruce and the spider). Unawares means without warning; to suffer someone to do something is to allow it.
readings.contentNote: Soldiers climb into a castle and fight, and many are killed; the mother and child are kept safe.

excerpt.locator: “The Black Douglas,” the whole story; opens “In Scotland, in the time of King Robert Bruce, there lived a brave man whose name was…”; closes “…and whether the mother made up any more songs about the Black Douglas I cannot tell.”.

questions.prompt: How did the Black Douglas get his name, and how did English mothers use it?
facilitatorNotes: From his long black hair and beard and dark face. Mothers told naughty children that the Black Douglas would get them, so his name had become a threat.
evidence: His hair and beard were black and long
the Black Douglas would get them

questions.prompt: What does the watchman think the dark shapes are? What are they really?
facilitatorNotes: The farmer’s cattle; really, Douglas and his men creeping on hands and feet, dragging ladders. Listeners learn the truth before anyone in the castle.
evidence: Those are nothing to frighten us.
But the dark objects were not cattle.

questions.prompt: Why is the woman’s song so surprising at that moment?
facilitatorNotes: She sings that the Black Douglas shall not get her child just as he stands behind her. The danger and the joke arrive together in his answer.
evidence: The Black Douglas shall not get ye.
Don't be so sure about that!

questions.prompt: How does the Black Douglas treat the woman and her child? Does that change your picture of him?
facilitatorNotes: He will not let anyone harm them. The man used to frighten children ends by protecting one. Some children will still see him as fierce; the last sentence leaves room for both views.
evidence: the Black Douglas would not suffer any one to harm them

readings.title: Other Wise Men of Gotham
readings.challenge: Explain why characters pretend to be foolish, and how listeners can tell.
readings.focus: The people of Gotham save their noses by acting like fools in front of the king’s sheriff.
readings.context: Gotham is a real village in England, famous in old jokes for its foolish people; a school night told of three of them. A sheriff was the king’s officer in charge of a county; lodging is a place to stay. The king in this story is not named.

excerpt.locator: “Other Wise Men of Gotham,” the whole story; opens “One day, news was brought to Gotham that the king was coming that way, and that he would…”; closes “…that if that was the case, he would not harm them, but would let them keep their noses.”.

questions.prompt: Why don’t the men of Gotham want the king to come to their town?
facilitatorNotes: He is cruel; they would have to feed and house all his men; and he would take whatever pleased him.
evidence: if he saw anything that pleased him, he would be sure to take it for his own

questions.prompt: What is Dobbin’s plan, and what reason does he give for it?
facilitatorNotes: Everyone should act like fools, because he has known men punished for being wise but never for being foolish. It is a wise idea about seeming foolish.
evidence: Many a man has been punished because he was wise, but I have never heard of any one being harmed because he was a fool.

questions.prompt: Pick one silly thing the sheriff sees. Why is it silly, and why is it also clever of the people of Gotham?
facilitatorNotes: Rolling stones uphill to make the sun rise, walling in a cuckoo, or carrying a door to guard money left at home. Each is silly as an act but clever as a performance, and each ends by praising the sheriff.
evidence: We are rolling stones up-hill to make the sun rise
we are building a wall around it
if I have the door with me, they can't break it open

questions.prompt: Who is really the wise one in this story?
facilitatorNotes: The people who pretend; the sheriff only thinks he is wise. His reply to the young men who “do the grunting” may even be a joke about the whole world. Children can argue for the sheriff, too: he decides not to hurt anyone.
evidence: we do the grunting while our fathers do the working
Well, that is the way the world goes every-where.
It would be a shame to harm such simple people.

readings.title: Sir Philip Sidney and The Ungrateful Soldier
readings.challenge: Compare two stories that use the same words but end differently.
readings.focus: Two soldiers give water to a dying enemy or comrade; one gift is answered with a bullet.
readings.context: Sir Philip Sidney was an English poet and soldier who died of a battle wound in 1586. Baldwin follows his story with a second one about a war between Sweden and Denmark. Wistful means longing; a flask is a small bottle; a knight or nobleman is given a title such as “Sir.”
readings.contentNote: Both stories take place on battlefields among wounded and dying soldiers; in the second, a wounded man shoots at the soldier who helps him.

excerpt.locator: “Sir Philip Sidney” and “The Ungrateful Soldier,” two whole stories that Baldwin prints together; opens “A cruel battle was being fought. The ground was covered with dead and dying men. The air…”; closes “…the king. And he re-ward-ed him by making him a knight, and giving him a noble title.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Sir Philip give away the water he needs himself?
facilitatorNotes: He sees a dying soldier’s wistful look and says that man needs it more. Sidney is badly wounded and thirsty too, which makes the gift a costly one.
evidence: The wist-ful look in the poor man's face spoke plainer than words.
Thy need is greater than mine.

questions.prompt: Baldwin says the second story is “much like” the first. What is the same, and what is different?
facilitatorNotes: In both, a wounded man is given a drink with the very same words. But the Swede repays the kindness by shooting, and the first story ends in mourning while the second ends in a reward.
evidence: much like the one which I have just told you
He pulled a pistol from his pocket

questions.prompt: The Dane says he will punish the Swede. What is the punishment, and is it really one?
facilitatorNotes: He drinks half and gives the Swede the other half. It is almost a joke of a punishment: he still helps him. Some children call it fair; others think the Swede deserved nothing.
evidence: now you shall have only half

questions.prompt: Why does the king make the Dane a nobleman?
facilitatorNotes: Because he “could never kill a wounded enemy.” The king honors mercy, not only courage. Ask what “noble” seems to mean in these two stories.
evidence: I could never kill a wounded enemy.
Then you deserve to be a no-ble-man

readings.title: Sir Humphrey Gilbert
readings.challenge: Think about what one sentence spoken in danger shows about a person.
readings.focus: Lost among icebergs, an explorer reads calmly and cheers his men.
readings.context: Sir Humphrey Gilbert was an English explorer who tried to start a settlement in North America; his ship was lost in 1583. Baldwin wrote in the 1890s for American children, so “this country of ours” means the United States. The Squirrel and the Golden Hind were Gilbert’s two ships.
readings.contentNote: Baldwin calls the Native peoples of America “wild Indians” and names them alongside wild beasts, a way of writing common in his time and unfair to them. The story ends with a ship lost at sea with everyone aboard.

excerpt.locator: “Sir Humphrey Gilbert,” the whole story; opens “More than three hundred years ago there lived in England a brave man whose name was Sir…”; closes “…vessel, with brave Sir Humphrey and all his brave men, was swal-lowed up by the waves.”.

questions.prompt: Baldwin writes that there were “no white people” in America then. Who did live there, and what do you notice about how he describes them?
facilitatorNotes: Many Native nations; Baldwin calls them “wild Indians” and lists them with wild beasts, as though they were part of the wilderness. Adults can explain that his words show how many people of his time thought. Children may notice that putting people beside beasts makes them seem less like people.
evidence: roamed wild In-di-ans and wild beasts

questions.prompt: What danger surrounds the ships after the wind dies and the cold comes?
facilitatorNotes: Great white icebergs drift in until the little ships are almost lost among “floating mountains of ice.”
evidence: the little ships were almost lost among the floating mountains of ice

questions.prompt: What does Sir Humphrey call to the other ship, and what do you think he means?
facilitatorNotes: “We are as near heaven on the sea as on the land.” He means that God is as close at sea as at home, so they need not be afraid. Some children hear courage; others hear that he knows he may die.
evidence: We are as near heaven on the sea as on the land.

questions.prompt: How do the men on the Golden Hind learn that the Squirrel is gone?
facilitatorNotes: They see its lights go out on a stormy night. The story tells the loss quietly, through one small detail.
evidence: All at once the men on the "Hind" saw the lights on board of the "Squirrel" go out.

readings.title: Sir Walter Raleigh
readings.challenge: Tell a famous story apart from the storyteller’s own opinion at the end.
readings.focus: A young man’s spoiled cloak wins a queen’s favour, and two plants from America reach England.
readings.context: Sir Walter Raleigh was a favourite of Queen Elizabeth I of England in the 1580s and the half-brother of Sir Humphrey Gilbert; the cloak story is an old legend. A queen’s train is the group of people who walk with her; a gentlewoman is a lady who serves her.
readings.contentNote: Baldwin, writing in the 1890s, calls Native Americans “savage Indians,” a phrase now recognized as unfair to them.

excerpt.locator: “Sir Walter Raleigh,” the whole story; opens “There once lived in England a brave and noble man whose name was Walter Ra-leigh. He was…”; closes “…countries of the world. It would have been well if Sir Walter Raleigh had let it alone.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Raleigh spread his cloak over the puddle, and what does it cost him?
facilitatorNotes: He forgets himself and thinks only of helping the queen across. He loses his beautiful scarlet cloak and has none to wear when she sends for him.
evidence: He took off his scarlet cloak, and spread it across the puddle.
he had no scarlet cloak to wear

questions.prompt: Which two plants did Raleigh bring to England from America, and who had shown how to use them?
facilitatorNotes: The potato and tobacco. The Indians already used both; the knowledge came from the people living there.
evidence: One was the po-ta-to, the other was to-bac-co.
He told his friends how the Indians used them for food

questions.prompt: Why does Raleigh’s servant throw a pail of water in his face?
facilitatorNotes: He sees smoke curling over his master’s head and thinks he is on fire. No one in England had seen anyone smoke before, so the mistake makes sense.
evidence: he thought that he was on fire

questions.prompt: The last sentence gives Baldwin’s own opinion. What is it, and how is it different from the rest of the story?
facilitatorNotes: That Raleigh would have done better to leave tobacco alone. It is the storyteller speaking to readers, not part of the events. Children can say why he might think so; smoking harms health.
evidence: It would have been well if Sir Walter Raleigh had let it alone.

readings.title: Pocahontas
readings.challenge: Notice when a storyteller warns that a tale may not be true, and ask whose side of it we hear.
readings.focus: A girl stops an execution by putting herself between a prisoner and the clubs.
readings.context: Captain John Smith was a leader of the English settlement at Jamestown, Virginia, which began in 1607. Pocahontas was a daughter of Powhatan, the leader of many Native nations there. Smith told this story years afterwards; historians are not sure it happened the way he told it.
readings.contentNote: A prisoner is about to be killed with clubs. Baldwin, like many writers of his time, shows the Powhatan people mainly as a danger to the English.

excerpt.locator: “Pocahontas,” the whole story; opens “There was once a very brave man whose name was John Smith. He came to this country many…”; closes “…was the friend of the white men, and she did a great many things to help them.”.

questions.prompt: Before the story begins, what does Baldwin say about the tales of John Smith?
facilitatorNotes: Some are true and some untrue, and this is the most famous. Ask what we would need to know to decide whether it really happened.
evidence: Many tales are told of his ad-ven-tures, some of them true and some of them untrue.

questions.prompt: What does Pocahontas do to save Smith?
facilitatorNotes: She rushes in, throws herself between him and the raised clubs and lays her head on his. The men cannot strike without hurting her.
evidence: She ran and threw herself between Smith and the up-lift-ed clubs.
they did not want to hurt the child

questions.prompt: What reason does Pocahontas give her father?
facilitatorNotes: Smith has done him no harm, and they ought to be his friends. She asks for friendship, not only pity.
evidence: I am sure he has done you no harm, and we ought to be his friends.

questions.prompt: This story comes from John Smith, an Englishman. What might Powhatan’s people have told differently?
facilitatorNotes: They might explain why the stranger was a prisoner, whether he was really about to die, or what the ceremony meant to them. A good answer notices that we hear only Smith’s side, retold by Baldwin. We are never told what the king himself was thinking. Children may also simply admire the girl’s courage.
evidence: The king at first did not know what to do.

readings.title: George Washington and His Hatchet
readings.challenge: Think about a story that teaches honesty even though it may never have happened.
readings.focus: A boy confesses to chopping down his father’s cherry tree, and his father forgives him.
readings.context: George Washington was the first President of the United States. This story was first printed by Mason Locke Weems in a book about Washington’s life written after he died, and most historians think Weems made it up. A falsehood is a lie.

excerpt.locator: “George Washington and His Hatchet,” the whole story; opens “When George Wash-ing-ton was quite a little boy, his father gave him a hatchet. It was…”; closes “…it. I would rather lose a dozen cherry trees than that you should tell one false-hood."”.

questions.prompt: Why did George chop down the tree?
facilitatorNotes: He had a bright new hatchet and thought it would be fine sport to see a tree fall, as he had seen his father’s men do. He did not mean harm; he wanted to try it.
evidence: it would be fine sport to see this tree fall with a crash to the ground

questions.prompt: How can you tell how angry George’s father is?
facilitatorNotes: He cries out that it was the only tree of its kind and cost a great deal, and he begins a threat he never finishes. The unfinished sentence leaves listeners wondering what he would have done.
evidence: It was the only tree of its kind in this country
I would—yes, I would

questions.prompt: Why does the father forget his anger?
facilitatorNotes: Because George told the truth. He says he would rather lose a dozen cherry trees than hear one lie. Ask whether every parent would answer the same way.
evidence: I would rather lose a dozen cherry trees than that you should tell one false-hood.

questions.prompt: Many people think this story was made up. Can a made-up story still teach something true?
facilitatorNotes: Some children will say yes: the lesson about honesty holds even if the event did not happen. Others may find it strange to teach honesty with an invented story. Both views are worth hearing.
evidence: I will tell you the truth about it.

readings.title: The Story of William Tell
readings.challenge: Follow the reasons behind a ruler’s cruel order, and decide what a second arrow means.
readings.focus: A proud hunter will not bow to a tyrant’s cap and is forced to shoot an apple from his son’s head.
readings.context: William Tell is a hero of Swiss legend, said to have lived about seven hundred years ago, when Switzerland was ruled by Austrian governors. A tyrant is a ruler who uses power cruelly and unfairly; to rebel is to rise up against a ruler.
readings.contentNote: A father is forced to shoot at an apple on his son’s head, and soldiers are ordered to kill the boy if he misses; the story ends by saying Tell later shot the tyrant.

excerpt.locator: “The Story of William Tell,” the whole story; opens “The people of Swit-zer-land were not always free and happy as they are to-day. Many years…”; closes “…this, Tell did shoot the tyrant with one of his arrows; and thus he set his country free.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Gessler order everyone to bow to a cap on a pole?
facilitatorNotes: The cap stands for him; bowing to it means obeying him. Tell’s folded arms and laughter show that he will not.
evidence: He would not bow down to Gessler himself.

questions.prompt: Why is Gessler’s punishment especially cruel?
facilitatorNotes: He turns Tell’s own great skill against him and puts his child in danger. The story says he meant the hunter’s skill to bring him to grief.
evidence: to make the hunter's own skill bring him to grief

questions.prompt: How does Tell’s son behave, and why?
facilitatorNotes: He stands firm and still, unafraid, because he trusts his father. His calm helps the shot go true.
evidence: He was not afraid, for he had all faith in his father's skill.

questions.prompt: What does the second arrow tell us about Tell?
facilitatorNotes: He had planned to shoot Gessler if he hurt his son. Some children admire his courage; others are troubled that he planned to kill. The story’s ending treats him as a hero who freed his country.
evidence: this arrow was for your heart if I had hurt my child

readings.title: Arnold Winkelried
readings.challenge: Explain how one person’s action changes a whole battle.
readings.focus: A farmer with no weapon breaks an army’s wall of spears so that his friends can win.
readings.context: This Swiss legend is told about the Battle of Sempach in 1386, when Swiss country people fought an Austrian army. Ranks and lines are rows of soldiers; scythes and pitchforks are farm tools; liberty means freedom.
readings.contentNote: Winkelried runs onto the soldiers’ spears and is killed so that his side can win the battle.

excerpt.locator: “Arnold Winkelried,” the whole story; opens “A great army was marching into Swit-zer-land. If it should go much farther, there would…”; closes “…ever knew before. But Switzerland was saved, and Arnold Wink-el-ried did not die in vain.”.

questions.prompt: Why can’t the Swiss arrows and stones harm the soldiers?
facilitatorNotes: The soldiers march close together, shields overlapping and spears bristling, so arrows glance off and stones do nothing.
evidence: their shields lapped over one another
their thousand spears looked like so many long bris-tles in the sun-light

questions.prompt: What does Winkelried say about his home before he runs forward? Why say it then?
facilitatorNotes: His wife and children are waiting for him, but they will not see him again. He knows what his plan will cost, and he names what he is fighting for.
evidence: There my wife and chil-dren wait for my return. But they will not see me again

questions.prompt: How does his run break the soldiers’ lines?
facilitatorNotes: The soldiers turn their spears to catch him and forget to keep their places, and his friends rush into the gap.
evidence: The soldiers forgot to stay in their places.

questions.prompt: The story ends, “Arnold Winkelried did not die in vain.” What does that mean, and do you agree?
facilitatorNotes: In vain means for nothing; his death opened the way to victory. Children may agree, or may think about the family waiting on the mountain; both are fair responses.
evidence: Arnold Wink-el-ried did not die in vain.

readings.title: How Napoleon Crossed the Alps
readings.challenge: Decide what a leader’s short sentences tell us about him.
readings.focus: A general refuses to hear that a march over the snowy mountains is impossible.
readings.context: Napoleon Bonaparte led the army of France about two hundred years ago (Baldwin wrote “about a hundred years ago” in 1896). The Alps are high, snowy mountains between France and Italy; a pass is a way through mountains; cannon are big guns pulled on wheels.

excerpt.locator: “How Napoleon Crossed the Alps,” the whole story; opens “About a hundred years ago there lived a great gen-er-al whose name was Na-po´le-on…”; closes “…man who has made up his mind to win," said Napoleon, "will never say 'Im-pos-si-ble.'"”.

questions.prompt: The scout begins, “It may be possible, but”—and Napoleon stops him. What do you think the scout was going to say?
facilitatorNotes: Probably that it would be very hard or dangerous: snow, cliffs, no road. Napoleon does not want to hear the reasons not to go.
evidence: It may be possible, but
Let me hear no more

questions.prompt: Why did people laugh at the plan?
facilitatorNotes: Sixty thousand men, with horses and cannon, were to cross mountains where there was no road. It sounded foolish.
evidence: People laughed at the thought of an army of sixty thousand men crossing the Alps where there was no road.

questions.prompt: What happens when the army reaches a place where there seems to be no way on?
facilitatorNotes: The trumpets sound “Charge!” and every man does his best, so the whole army keeps moving. Ask whether the trumpets or the men did the work.
evidence: the trum-pets sounded "Charge!" Then every man did his best

questions.prompt: Napoleon says a person who has made up his mind to win will never say “Impossible.” Is he right?
facilitatorNotes: He was right this time. Children may also think of times when listening to a warning is wise; the scout may have had good reasons. Both views are fair.
evidence: will never say 'Im-pos-si-ble.'

readings.title: The Story of Cincinnatus
readings.challenge: Follow bad news from a faraway valley to a farmer’s field.
readings.focus: A poor farmer is given all the power in Rome, saves the city, and gives the power back.
readings.context: This is an old Roman legend. The “Fathers” were the old men who made Rome’s laws. To till the soil is to farm it; plundering means robbing; a pass is a narrow way between mountains; entrapped means caught in a trap.
readings.contentNote: Soldiers are killed in the fighting. Baldwin calls the mountain tribe “savage” and “half-wild,” the way old Roman stories spoke of Rome’s enemies.

excerpt.locator: “The Story of Cincinnatus,” the whole story; opens “There was a man named Cin-cin-na´tus who lived on a little farm not far from the city of…”; closes “He had been the ruler of Rome for sixteen days.”.

questions.prompt: What do the neighbors always say when someone is in trouble?
facilitatorNotes: “Go and tell Cincinnatus. He will help you.” Later the Fathers say almost the same words, so the story shows his reputation reaching all the way to the rulers.
evidence: Go and tell Cincinnatus. He will help you.
Send for Cincinnatus. He will help us.

questions.prompt: How was the Roman army caught in a trap?
facilitatorNotes: It was in a narrow valley; the mountain men blocked the way in front and behind and threw rocks from above, so the soldiers could not fight or go back.
evidence: The fierce men of the mountains were before us and behind us

questions.prompt: What is Cincinnatus doing when the messengers come, and what does he do first?
facilitatorNotes: Plowing his field. He greets them kindly, asks whether all is well with Rome, and puts on his cloak to hear them. He thinks of Rome before himself.
evidence: Is all well with Rome?

questions.prompt: Why were some people afraid of Cincinnatus, and what does he do that shows they need not have been?
facilitatorNotes: He had all the power in Rome and could have made himself king. Instead he gave the power back after sixteen days and went home to his plow. Ask why that might be harder than winning the battle.
evidence: he had all power in Rome to do what he pleased
he gave back the power to the white-haired Roman Fathers

readings.title: The Story of Regulus
readings.challenge: Weigh a promise against what a person loves most.
readings.focus: A Roman general keeps his word to his enemies, though it means leaving his family for prison.
readings.context: Rome and Carthage, a great city across the sea in Africa, fought long wars more than two thousand years ago. A prisoner of war is a soldier held by the enemy. Bade them good-by means said goodbye to them.
readings.contentNote: Regulus goes back to Carthage knowing he will be put to death; the story names his “cruel death” but does not describe it. His family weeps at the parting.

excerpt.locator: “The Story of Regulus,” the whole story; opens “On the other side of the sea from Rome there was once a great city named Car-thage. The…”; closes “This was the kind of courage that made Rome the greatest city in the world.”.

questions.prompt: What two things does Carthage make Regulus promise?
facilitatorNotes: To tell the Romans the war is going badly for them, and to come back to prison if they will not make peace.
evidence: you must promise us, that, if they will not make peace, you will come back to your prison

questions.prompt: Why do the men of Carthage let him go?
facilitatorNotes: They know that a great Roman keeps his word. His good name is what sets him free.
evidence: for they knew that a great Roman would keep his word

questions.prompt: What does Regulus tell the Fathers about making peace? Is that what Carthage wanted?
facilitatorNotes: The opposite: he tells them to keep fighting because Carthage is afraid and Rome is winning. He keeps his promise to return, but he tells the truth about the war.
evidence: But it will not be wise to make peace.

questions.prompt: His sons beg him to stay. Should he keep his promise? Talk about both sides.
facilitatorNotes: Regulus says a Roman must keep his word, and the story praises his courage. Many children will feel for his family and think the promise was made to enemies; let them say why. The story’s answer and theirs may differ.
evidence: Shall a Roman not keep his word?
His wife and little children wept

readings.title: Androclus and the Lion
readings.challenge: Notice how one act of kindness is repaid years later.
readings.focus: A runaway slave pulls a thorn from a lion’s paw, and the lion remembers him in the arena.
readings.context: In ancient Rome some people were slaves, owned by masters and forced to work. Crowds watched fights in great arenas, which Baldwin compares to a circus or a ball game. Befriended means was a friend to; liberty means freedom.
readings.contentNote: By the law of the time, a runaway slave is made to face a hungry lion before a crowd that expects to see him killed. No one is hurt.

excerpt.locator: “Androclus and the Lion,” the whole story; opens “In Rome there was once a poor slave whose name was An´dro-clus. His master was a cruel…”; closes “…the lion was given to him for his own. And they lived together in Rome for many years.”.

questions.prompt: How does Androclus know the lion is not angry?
facilitatorNotes: It limps as though its foot hurts, stands still, and rubs its head against his shoulder.
evidence: he limped as though his foot hurt him

questions.prompt: What does the lion do after the thorn comes out?
facilitatorNotes: Jumps about like a dog, licks Androclus’s hands and feet, sleeps beside him, and brings him food every day.
evidence: He jumped about like a dog

questions.prompt: Androclus gives a great cry in the arena, “not of fear, but of gladness.” Why gladness?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes the hungry lion as his friend from the cave.
evidence: Androclus gave a great cry, not of fear, but of gladness.

questions.prompt: Androclus says, “no man has ever befriended me.” What does the crowd learn, and how does it change?
facilitatorNotes: That a lion was kinder to him than any person. The people who came to see him killed shout for his freedom. Ask whether the lion taught the crowd something about kindness.
evidence: This poor lion alone has been kind to me
Live and be free!

readings.title: Horatius at the Bridge
readings.challenge: Follow two things happening at once on either side of a bridge.
readings.focus: One Roman guard holds back an army while his friends chop down the bridge behind him.
readings.context: This is an old Roman legend. The Tiber is the river that flows through Rome. To keep the foe at bay is to hold the enemy back; to hew is to chop. The verses come from a famous poem about Horatius by Thomas Babington Macaulay; spake means spoke.
readings.contentNote: A soldier’s dart puts out Horatius’s left eye, and spears are thrown at him as he swims.

excerpt.locator: “Horatius at the Bridge,” the whole story, with its lines of verse; opens “Once there was a war between the Roman people and the E-trus´cans who lived in the towns…”; closes “…Still was the story told, How well Horatius kept the bridge In the brave days of old."”.

questions.prompt: Why must the bridge come down?
facilitatorNotes: If the Etruscans cross it, the Romans cannot stop them, and the city will be lost.
evidence: If they once gain the bridge, we cannot hinder them from crossing

questions.prompt: What are the Romans doing behind Horatius while he fights?
facilitatorNotes: Chopping at the beams and posts with axes until the bridge trembles and falls. The two scenes happen at the same time.
evidence: Their axes rang, the chips flew fast

questions.prompt: What does Horatius tell his two friends to do, and why do you think he stays?
facilitatorNotes: To run for their lives while he keeps the road. Someone has to hold the horsemen back until the bridge falls; he takes the greatest danger himself.
evidence: Run for your lives!
I will keep the road.

questions.prompt: Even Porsena’s men cheer when Horatius reaches the bank. Why would enemies cheer?
facilitatorNotes: They had never seen anyone so brave and strong, and they could not help praising the deed even though it beat them. Children may find this surprising; ask what it says about courage.
evidence: Then Porsena's men shouted also
he had done a deed which they could not help but praise

readings.title: Julius Cæsar
readings.challenge: Put two short episodes together to describe one person.
readings.focus: A proud mayor and a frightened boat captain show what Cæsar thought about greatness.
readings.context: Julius Cæsar was a Roman general who made himself ruler of Rome about two thousand years ago. The old letter æ in his name sounds like “ee.” A mayor is the head of a town; to strut is to walk proudly.

excerpt.locator: “Julius Cæsar,” the whole story; opens “Nearly two thousand years ago there lived in Rome a man whose name was Julius Cæ´sar. He…”; closes “…should you be afraid?" he said. "The boat will not be lost; for you have Cæsar on board."”.

questions.prompt: Why do Cæsar’s officers laugh at the village mayor?
facilitatorNotes: He is proud and happy leading only about fifty people, so they think he is silly. They call his villagers his “little flock.”
evidence: See how that fellow struts at the head of his little flock!

questions.prompt: Cæsar would rather be the head man of a village than the second man in Rome. What does that tell you about him?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to be first, wherever it is; being second, even in a great city, would not satisfy him. Some children may admire this; others may think it shows too much pride.
evidence: I would rather be the head man of a village than the second man in Rome!

questions.prompt: How do the captain and Cæsar act differently in the storm?
facilitatorNotes: The captain trembles, falls on his knees and moans that all is lost; Cæsar is not afraid and tells him to take the oars again.
evidence: All is lost! all is lost!
But Cæsar was not afraid.

questions.prompt: “You have Cæsar on board.” Is that a good reason not to be afraid of a storm?
facilitatorNotes: A storm does not know who is in the boat, so it is not really a reason. But his confidence may have helped the captain row again. The story asks us to answer “Why was he so great?”; let children decide whether this is greatness or boasting.
evidence: for you have Cæsar on board.
Why was he so great?

readings.title: The Sword of Damocles
readings.challenge: Explain a lesson that is shown, not told, by one object.
readings.focus: A man who envies a king learns, under a hanging sword, what the king’s life is really like.
readings.context: This old Greek story is so well known that people still say a danger hangs “like the sword of Damocles.” A tyrant is a cruel ruler; dread is great fear; a banquet is a feast; a cottage is a small house.

excerpt.locator: “The Sword of Damocles,” the whole story; opens “There was once a king whose name was Di-o-nys´i-us. He was so unjust and cruel that he…”; closes “…he never again wanted to be rich, or to change places, even for a moment, with the king.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Damocles think the king must be happy?
facilitatorNotes: The king is rich, lives in a fine palace full of beautiful things, and has many servants.
evidence: You have here everything that any man could wish.

questions.prompt: What does Damocles see above his head, and what holds it there?
facilitatorNotes: A sharp sword hanging by a single horse-hair, with its point almost touching his head.
evidence: It was a sharp sword, and it was hung by only a single horse-hair.

questions.prompt: How does Damocles change once he sees the sword? Find the words that show it.
facilitatorNotes: His smile fades, his face goes pale, his hands tremble, and he cannot enjoy the food, wine or music any more.
evidence: The smile faded from the lips of Damocles.
He wanted no more food

questions.prompt: The king says he has a sword over his head all the time. What is his sword?
facilitatorNotes: Not a real sword: his fear that someone will kill him, because so many people hate him. Children may add that being cruel made the danger. Damocles decides the rich and powerful are not so happy as they seem.
evidence: I have a sword over my head all the time.
the rich and pow-er-ful are not so happy as they seem

readings.title: Damon and Pythias
readings.challenge: Follow a friendship tested by time running out.
readings.focus: A man takes his friend’s place in prison, trusting him to come back before the day of death.
readings.context: This is an old Greek story about the same tyrant Dionysius who appears in “The Sword of Damocles.” Affairs are business and duties; in his stead means in his place; hindered means held back.
readings.contentNote: Pythias is sentenced to death, and Damon offers to die in his place; in the end both are freed.

excerpt.locator: “Damon and Pythias,” the whole story; opens “A young man whose name was Pyth´i-as had done something which the tyrant Dionysius did…”; closes “"I would give all my wealth to have one such friend," he said.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the tyrant laugh at Pythias?
facilitatorNotes: He does not believe that a man set free would ever come back to die.
evidence: How can I know that you will keep your promise?

questions.prompt: What does Damon offer, and why is he so sure?
facilitatorNotes: To be put in prison in his friend’s place and to die if Pythias does not return. He knows Pythias has never broken his word.
evidence: he is a man who has never broken his word

questions.prompt: When Pythias is late, what does Damon say about it?
facilitatorNotes: That if Pythias does not come back, it will not be his fault: something will have stopped him. Damon keeps trusting even when time is almost gone.
evidence: If Pythias does not come back in time, it will not be his fault.

questions.prompt: Why does the tyrant set them both free? Has he changed?
facilitatorNotes: He sees that friends who trust each other like this ought not to suffer, and he wishes he had such a friend. Some children may say he has changed a little; others that he is still a tyrant who just admires them.
evidence: I would give all my wealth to have one such friend

readings.title: A Laconic Answer
readings.challenge: Explain how a one-word answer can say a great deal.
readings.focus: The Spartans answer a king’s threat with a single word.
readings.context: Greece was once made up of separate states. The Spartans lived in a land called Laconia, so “laconic” came to mean using very few words. To level a city is to knock it flat.

excerpt.locator: “A Laconic Answer,” the whole story; opens “Many miles beyond Rome there was a famous country which we call Greece. The people of…”; closes “…as to say, "We are not afraid of you so long as the little word 'if' stands in your way."”.

questions.prompt: What strange rule did the Spartans have about speaking?
facilitatorNotes: To speak briefly and never use more words than were needed.
evidence: they should speak briefly, and never use more words than were needed

questions.prompt: What does King Philip threaten?
facilitatorNotes: That if he goes into their country, he will level their great city to the ground.
evidence: If I go down into your country, I will level your great city to the ground.

questions.prompt: The Spartans answer only “IF.” What are they telling him?
facilitatorNotes: That he has not come yet, and they are not afraid while that little word stands in his way: he will have to win first. Ask children to say the long answer the one word stands for.
evidence: It was as much as to say, "We are not afraid of you so long as the little word 'if' stands in your way."

questions.prompt: Is a short answer braver than a long one? Why might it be?
facilitatorNotes: A short answer sounds calm and unafraid; a long one could sound worried. Some children may think a long, clear answer could be just as brave.
evidence: That word was "IF."

readings.title: The Ungrateful Guest
readings.challenge: Name the moment a character chooses to break a promise.
readings.focus: A soldier saved by a farmer takes the farmer’s land, and the king punishes him.
readings.context: King Philip is the same king of Macedon who threatened the Spartans in “A Laconic Answer.” Churlish means rude and mean; base means low and shameful; to shun is to keep away from someone.
readings.contentNote: As punishment the king has the words “The Ungrateful Guest” burned into the soldier’s forehead.

excerpt.locator: “The Ungrateful Guest,” the whole story; opens “Among the soldiers of King Philip there was a poor man who had done some brave deeds. He…”; closes “…tried to enrich himself; and from that day until he died all men shunned and hated him.”.

questions.prompt: What does the farmer do for the soldier, and what does the soldier promise?
facilitatorNotes: He saves him when he is cast half-drowned on the shore and cares for him; the soldier promises to repay him.
evidence: promised that he would repay him for his kindness

questions.prompt: How does the soldier describe the farmer to the king? Is it true?
facilitatorNotes: As a churlish farmer who has never done anything for his country. It is false: the farmer saved one of the king’s soldiers.
evidence: Only a churlish farmer, who has never done anything for his country

questions.prompt: What does the farmer do when he loses his home, and what does that tell you about him?
facilitatorNotes: He goes boldly to the king and tells the whole story. He is brave enough to speak to a king about a wrong done to him.
evidence: He went boldly to the king, and told the whole story from beginning to end.

questions.prompt: Why is “guest” a good word for the soldier, and why is his punishment written on his face?
facilitatorNotes: He was the farmer’s guest, cared for in his house, and then repaid him with harm. Writing it on his forehead lets everyone know what he did. Children may find the punishment harsh; let them say whether they think it fits.
evidence: THE UNGRATEFUL GUEST.
all the world was made to know of the mean act

readings.title: The Brave Three Hundred
readings.challenge: Explain why a small number of people could hold back a huge army.
readings.focus: Three hundred Spartans guard a narrow pass against the army of Persia.
readings.context: This happened at Thermopylae in Greece in 480 B.C. Persia was a great empire to the east. Earth and water were signs that a land would obey the Persian king. A pass is a narrow way; to keep at bay is to hold back; the slain are the dead.
readings.contentNote: This is a battle story: the Spartans fight with spears, swords, daggers and even fists and teeth, and all of them are killed. The story praises their dying for their country.

excerpt.locator: “The Brave Three Hundred,” the whole story; opens “All Greece was in danger. A mighty army, led by the great King of Persia, had come from…”; closes “…tell the story of Leonidas and the brave three hundred who died for their country's sake.”.

questions.prompt: What does the King of Persia ask for, and what do the Greeks answer?
facilitatorNotes: Earth and water, as a sign that their land and sea are his. They answer that they will be free.
evidence: No: we will be free.

questions.prompt: Why could three hundred men hold the pass at all?
facilitatorNotes: The pass was the only way in and very narrow, between the mountains and the sea, so the huge army could not all fight at once.
evidence: a narrow pass between the mountains and the sea

questions.prompt: When they hear the Persian arrows will darken the sun, the Spartans say, “we shall fight in the shade.” What does that answer show?
facilitatorNotes: They joke instead of showing fear. It is a laconic answer, like the Spartans’ “IF” in an earlier story.
evidence: So much the better
we shall fight in the shade.

questions.prompt: The Spartans all die, yet the story says Greece was saved. How can both be true?
facilitatorNotes: They held the Persians back all day and killed many, which helped Greece. Some children may feel the ending is sad more than glorious; both feelings belong to this story.
evidence: And Greece was saved.
there was not one Spartan left alive

readings.title: The King and His Hawk
readings.challenge: Look back at a character’s actions once you learn something new.
readings.focus: A thirsty king kills the hawk that keeps spilling his water, then finds out why it did.
readings.context: Genghis Khan was a Mongol ruler who conquered a huge empire about eight hundred years ago. Hunters trained hawks to catch game for them. Trickling means falling a little at a time.
readings.contentNote: In anger the king strikes his hawk with his sword, and it dies at his feet. A dead poisonous snake lies in the spring.

excerpt.locator: “The King and His Hawk,” the whole story; opens “Gen´ghis Khan was a great king and war-rior.”; closes “"I have learned a sad lesson to-day; and that is, never to do any-thing in anger."”.

questions.prompt: Why does it take so long to fill the cup?
facilitatorNotes: The summer heat has dried up the brooks, and the water comes over the rock only one drop at a time.
evidence: now it came only one drop at a time

questions.prompt: How many times does the hawk knock the cup away, and how does the king feel each time?
facilitatorNotes: Four times. He grows angry, then very angry, and the fourth time he strikes the hawk with his sword.
evidence: And now the king began to grow angry.
The king was now very angry indeed.

questions.prompt: What does the king find in the pool, and what does it change?
facilitatorNotes: A huge dead snake of the most poisonous kind. He understands that the hawk was keeping him from drinking poisoned water.
evidence: It was a huge, dead snake of the most poi-son-ous kind.
The hawk saved my life!

questions.prompt: The king says his lesson is “never to do any-thing in anger.” What else could he have done when the hawk kept spilling the cup?
facilitatorNotes: Stopped to wonder why his best hunting bird was acting so strangely, or looked at the water. Children may suggest other choices; the point is that anger kept him from thinking.
evidence: never to do any-thing in anger

readings.title: The Kingdoms
readings.challenge: Follow a riddle game whose last answer is a surprise.
readings.focus: A king plays a question game with children in a meadow, and the smallest gives the answer that moves him.
readings.context: Frederick William was a king of Prussia, a country that is now part of Germany. People once sorted all things into three “kingdoms”: animal, vegetable (plants) and mineral (stones and metals). The kingdom of heaven is a Christian phrase for God’s kingdom.

excerpt.locator: “The Kingdoms,” the whole story; opens “There was once a king of Prussia whose name was Frederick William.”; closes “…arms. Tears were in his eyes as he kissed her, and said, "So be it, my child! So be it."”.

questions.prompt: Why does the boy say the orange belongs to the vegetable kingdom?
facilitatorNotes: It is the fruit of a plant, and all plants belong to that kingdom.
evidence: It is the fruit of a plant, and all plants belong to that kingdom

questions.prompt: How do the children know which kingdom the gold piece belongs to?
facilitatorNotes: Gold is a metal, and all metals belong to the mineral kingdom.
evidence: All metals belong to that kingdom.

questions.prompt: Why are the bright boys puzzled by the last question?
facilitatorNotes: The king seems to want “the animal kingdom,” but that sounds rude to say to a grown man, and “the kingdom of Prussia” does not fit the game. They are afraid to answer.
evidence: Some wanted to say, "To the animal kingdom." But they were a little afraid

questions.prompt: Why do you think the little girl’s answer brings tears to the king’s eyes?
facilitatorNotes: She answers kindly and simply, as if she sees a good man rather than a king. Some children may say he is moved because she does not know he is a king; others that he hopes her answer is true. Accept reasons drawn from the story.
evidence: I think to the kingdom of heaven.
Tears were in his eyes

readings.title: The Barmecide Feast
readings.challenge: Watch two people pretend together, and ask why each one does it.
readings.focus: A rich man serves a starving beggar an imaginary supper, then a real one.
readings.context: This tale comes from the Arabian Nights, a famous old collection of stories. The Barmecide is a title for a rich lord. Schacabac’s religion forbids wine. A pretense is make-believe; sweetmeats are sweets.

excerpt.locator: “The Barmecide Feast,” the whole story; opens “There was once a rich old man who was called the Bar-me-cide. He lived in a beautiful…”; closes “…lived with the Barmecide many years, and never again knew what it was to be hungry.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Schacabac go to the Barmecide’s palace?
facilitatorNotes: He has had nothing to eat for two days and hopes the rich man will help him.
evidence: it was now two days since he had tasted bread

questions.prompt: What does Schacabac see when the Barmecide calls for water and supper?
facilitatorNotes: Nothing: no boy, no basin, no water and no food. The rich man only pretends, and Schacabac decides to pretend too.
evidence: Schacabac saw no boy, nor basin, nor water.

questions.prompt: How hungry is Schacabac while he pretends to eat, and why does he keep going?
facilitatorNotes: Almost dead with hunger, but too polite not to do as he is bidden. He also thinks he understands the joke.
evidence: Schacabac was almost dead with hunger, but he was too polite not to do as he was bidden.

questions.prompt: Was the pretend feast cruel or a test? What does the Barmecide say he has found?
facilitatorNotes: The Barmecide says Schacabac is a man of good understanding who makes the best of everything, and gives him a real supper and a home. Some children will still think it was unkind to tease a starving man; both views can be argued from the story.
evidence: I have found you to be a man of good un-der-stand-ing.
never again knew what it was to be hungry

readings.title: The Endless Tale
readings.challenge: Notice how a clever storyteller turns a king’s own wish against him.
readings.focus: A king who wants a story without an end gets one, and finds he did not want it after all.
readings.context: Baldwin printed hyphens inside longer words to help young readers sound them out. An heir is the one who will rule after the king; a granary is a storehouse for grain, and corn here means grain of any kind; a crevice is a narrow crack; a cubit is an old measure, about the length of a grown-up’s forearm.
readings.contentNote: The king says any storyteller who tries and fails will have his head cut off, and the story hints that one young man did. As in many old tales, the king’s daughter is offered as a prize.

excerpt.locator: “The Endless Tale,” the whole story; opens “In the Far East there was a great king who had no work to do. Every day, and all day…”; closes “…many years. But his father-in-law, the king, did not care to listen to any more stories.”.

questions.prompt: What is the one fault the king finds with every story?
facilitatorNotes: It is too short. A king with nothing to do wants stories to fill all his days.
evidence: it is too short

questions.prompt: Why do only a few young men try to win the prize?
facilitatorNotes: The hard condition: whoever tries and fails loses his head. The young man whose story lasted three months became “a warning to others.”
evidence: he shall have his head cut off
His fate was a warning to others

questions.prompt: How does the stranger make his story last for ever? Try telling it his way for a little while.
facilitatorNotes: He repeats one sentence, a locust carrying away one grain at a time, and the granary holds thousands of cubits of grain. Saying it aloud a few times shows how quickly it would wear a listener out.
evidence: then another locust went in and carried away a grain of corn
there are many thousand cubits in the granary

questions.prompt: Did the stranger win fairly, or by a trick? What has the king learned by the last sentence?
facilitatorNotes: The tale never ended, so he did what was asked, though not in the way the king meant. Some children call it clever, others a cheat. The king, who once found every story too short, no longer cares to hear any.
evidence: But do not let me hear another word about those horrible locusts!
did not care to listen to any more stories

readings.title: The Inchcape Rock
readings.challenge: Follow a cause from the start of a story to its end, and notice a wish that comes back.
readings.focus: A sea robber cuts away the bell that warns ships of a hidden rock, and later wrecks his own ship on it.
readings.context: The Inchcape Rock, also called the Bell Rock, is a real reef off the east coast of Scotland, and an old story says an abbot once hung a bell there; the poet Robert Southey told it in a ballad. An abbot is the head of an abbey, a home for monks; a buoy is a float fastened in the water to mark a danger; to plunder is to rob; breakers are waves breaking on rocks; the pilot steers the ship.
readings.contentNote: The robber’s ship strikes the rock and sinks, and he drowns.

excerpt.locator: “The Inchcape Rock,” the whole story; opens “In the North Sea there is a great rock called the Inch-cape Rock. It is twelve miles from…”; closes “…over him? Was it the abbot's bell, ringing for him far down at the bottom of the sea?”.

questions.prompt: Why does the abbot put a bell on the rock, and how does it ring with no one to ring it?
facilitatorNotes: So that sailors can hear where the hidden rock is and steer around it. The waves knock the floating buoy and ring the bell.
evidence: when the waves dashed against it, the bell would ring out loud and clear

questions.prompt: Why is the bell silent on the day Ralph the Rover sees it?
facilitatorNotes: The sea is as smooth as glass, so there are no waves to move it. The calm gives him time and the idea.
evidence: There were no waves to set it in motion.

questions.prompt: Ralph calls cutting the bell a trick. What does he expect to happen, and what does happen?
facilitatorNotes: He expects the next ship to wreck and curse the abbot instead of blessing him. Instead his own ship is the one that strikes the rock, and he calls himself a wretch.
evidence: The next one that comes this way will not bless the abbot
This is what comes of the joke that I played on the good abbot!

questions.prompt: In the fog Ralph says, “I wish we could hear the good abbot's bell.” Why is that wish so sad? What does the last question in the story suggest?
facilitatorNotes: He wishes for the very bell he destroyed. The ending imagines the bell ringing for him under the sea, like a bell for the dead, or like the sound of justice. Some children feel he got what he deserved; others feel sorry for the sailors who sank with him.
evidence: I wish we could hear the good abbot's bell.
ringing for him far down at the bottom of the sea

readings.title: Casabianca
readings.challenge: Notice how the storyteller changes the way he tells the story as it reaches its end.
readings.focus: A boy obeys his father’s order to stay at his post on a burning warship, not knowing that his father is already dead.
readings.context: Casabianca was a real boy, the son of the captain of a French warship. In 1798, in a battle near the mouth of the Nile in Egypt, the ship caught fire and blew up. Felicia Hemans wrote a poem about him nearly thirty years later, and generations of schoolchildren learned it by heart. The flag-ship carries the fleet’s commander; powder means gunpowder; the hold is the space below the deck; spars are the poles that carry the sails.
readings.contentNote: In a sea battle many men are killed, and the boy dies when the burning ship’s gunpowder explodes. His father had been killed at the start of the fight.

excerpt.locator: “Casabianca,” the whole story, with the opening stanzas of Mrs. Hemans’s poem that Baldwin quotes; opens “There was a great battle at sea. One could hear nothing but the roar of the big guns. The…”; closes “…As born to rule the storm— A creature of heroic blood, A proud though childlike form."”.

questions.prompt: Why won’t young Casabianca leave with the men in the boat?
facilitatorNotes: His father told him to stand at his post, he has been taught always to obey, and he trusts his father to tell him when to go.
evidence: When father bids me, I will go
he had been taught always to obey

questions.prompt: What does the boy not know that the reader knows?
facilitatorNotes: That his father lies dead in the cabin below, struck by a cannon ball at the very beginning of the fight. Only the reader knows no answer can come; the boy thinks he hears one.
evidence: a cannon ball had struck him dead at the very be-gin-ning of the fight
he fancied that his father's voice came faintly to him

questions.prompt: Near the end the story suddenly asks, “But what is that?” and tells the rest as if it were happening now. Why might Baldwin do that? Which earlier sentence warned us?
facilitatorNotes: The short sentences, the question and the “Boom!” put the listener on the ship at that moment. “There was powder in the hold” was said near the start, so the ending feels both sudden and expected.
evidence: But what is that?
There was powder in the hold!

questions.prompt: Was it brave or foolish for Casabianca to stay? Baldwin also says the famous poem is “not a very well written poem.” What do you think of each?
facilitatorNotes: Some children admire his loyalty; others think his father would have wanted him to live, and that obeying should have limits. Baldwin admires the boy but criticises the poem, so a story and a poem can be judged separately.
evidence: It is not a very well written poem
The boy stood on the burning deck
